title: FRCS Ophthalmology EXAM INSIGHTS: A Multi-Center Compendium (Amman & Mumbai 2024-2025)
summary: This comprehensive poster distills the experiences of multiple successful candidates who recently cleared the FRCS (Glasgow) Ophthalmology Part 3 exam in Amman and Mumbai. It offers a unique Q&A format, detailing OSCE and Viva scenarios, clinical examination cases, study resources, and invaluable advice for future aspirants, enriched with essential clinical pearls and management insights.

sections.title: Dr. Muhammad Ahsen's FRCS Experience (Amman, April 2024)
sections.content: I am Dr MUHAMMAD AHSEN from Pakistan. Did my FCPS training at Allied Hospital Faisalabad. MBBS, FCPS (ophth) FRCS (Glasgow) (ophth). Currently working in MOH-Kuwait. All praise to Allah Almighty, I have cleared FRCS Glasgow in my first attempt at Amman (Jordan) on April 24.

sections.title: Dr. Ahsen's Study Sources
content: 1. Kanski
2. Oxford Ophthalmology Handbook
3. Emergency Medicine Oxford Handbook
4. Past experiences at Amman Center.
5. Eye wiki on google :)

sections.title: OSCE (23-4-24) Highlights - Anterior Segment/Lids Adnexa/Oculoplastic
content: 1) Papilloma photo at lower lid. The First Examiner asked to describe findings and give differentials then possible diagnoses, causes, and treatment options.
2) After uneventful phaco surgery the patient has -2.00D refractive error. Causes, management options. Told all in detail for early and late management.
3) Scenario of a child with congenital ptosis +Marcus Gun Jaw winking phenomenon. Asked for management options.
4) Signs of PCR while phaco emulsification and management in each step detailed discussion.
5) Lattice dystrophy photo description & give differentials, usual symptoms of patients having lattice-like RCE management, and finally keratoplasty options.

6) Scenario of the patient having one-day old eye injury with broken glass. A detailed discussion of ruptured globe/IOFB management, investigations especially how to repair Corneo-Scleral tear. Where to apply first suture, which suture and exploration to look for the posterior extent of tear.

sections.title: OSCE (23-4-24) Highlights - Posterior Segment
content: 1) A photo of a thin avascular bleb overhanging limbus without PI in the photo may be the bleb was obscuring P.I. Particularly asked why the bleb is thin/avascular. I told could be due to the MMC application. Description of bleb, functional/non-functional bleb. Detailed discussion of post-trabeculectomy complications.
2) Photo of NVG with extensive rubeosis iridis, causes & management options. I stated that management depends on visual potential then discussed every possible scenario accordingly.

3) Humphery Visual field 24-2 photo with paracentral scotomas. Started describing reliability indices and the testing algorithms then he asked what is SITA FAST? why? Told the answer quicker/reliable and the bell rang.

4) Simply asked in BRVO what are your concerns in such patients? Told in detail about the causes and management of CME and systemic risk factors management to prevent ischemia and NVG in eye as well as cardiovascular complications.
5) Scenario of metamorphopsia and blurred vision in 80years old lady. Differentials and then discussion of macular hole management at all stages.
6) Retinitis pigmentosa fundus photo. Description and causes of poor vision in RP patients, told all causes from anterior segment to posterior segment.

sections.title: OSCE (23-4-24) Highlights - Neuro Motility and General Medicine
content: 1) Graves ophthalmopathy causes esp Patho physiology and systemic signs other than ocular features. Treatment options.

2) Typical scenario of IIH with fundus photo of papiledema. Investigations and management options. Don't forget to refer to neurology and neuropathologist for ON fenesteration or VP shunting by a neurosurgeon for persistent symptoms.
3) Scenario of patient having Grand mal seizures - causes and management.
4) Fundus photo of swollen optic disc with female having blurred vision and pain on eye movements.- Optic neuritis, causes other than demyelinating.

5) 40 year old male with sudden headache and unilateral ptosis but when he lifts his eyelid he complains of double vision. Dds: 3rd nerve palsy vs horner syndrome. Definite dx: 3rd nerve but examiner on my station was insisting for horner syndrome not in mood of discussing why its not horner. But i agreed at the end ok if you say its horner ok then let it be. But my top differential was 3rd nerve palsy. Then he asked the surgical and medical causes of 3rd nerve palsy and investigations.
6) Photo of intermittent exotropia with time to time outward deviation of eyes of 8 years old boy noted by the parents recently. Management options in detail.

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25-4-24) - Posterior Segment Cases
content: Case-1. Examine the posterior segment of left eye patient sitting on slit lamp. I started examining from anterior to posterior as the patient had corneal graft, aphakic and siliconized eye with flat retina and pale optic disc and peripheral laser marks. It was a case of post-op gunshot injury (ruptured globe + IOFB/RRD) Asked about the findings and status of retina attached or detached. Complications of silicon oil.

Case-2) command of posterior segment examination of left eye of old age male patient with indirect ophthalmoscope.. Pupil was mid dilated and patient was pseudophakic but with good view. It was post op PPV TRD/ VH with endolaser marks at peripheral retina and dull foveal reflex, pale optic disc + fibrous bands around disc. Usual questions of ppv indications and complications.

Case-3) A young boy sitting on a slit lamp with Stargadts disease with exotropia in right eye i just described optic disc (slight pallor) findings and a dull reflex of macula & the bell rang. Couldn’t complete the case and the examiner seemed satisfied already.

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25-4-24) - Neuro-Ophthalmic & Motility Disorders
sections.content:
Case-1: Young girl with glasses having Good alternating Esotropia. Command was to do the motility examination.. I started with VA-Hirschbergh-cover/ uncover @ distance and near with and without glasses. And finally, EOM with saccades and convergence. 6 minutes passed so quickly that just 1 question was asked: what's the diagnosis? I said alternating esotropia but i need to take history he said its since birth then I told ok its infantile esotropia. He asked what about the glasses , i said there could be refractive error. He nodded & examiner seemed satisfied.

Case-2: The worst case as i still couldnt understand what was the actual problem with that lady. 😛 a hard nut to crack! Middle aged lady sitting on slit lamp Command: Examine the pupils, anterior segment of both eyes and fundus exam in undilated Pupils. I Started off with dim light pupil examination and found bilateral brisk response pupils no RAPD, Just aniscoria in dark . right pupil was a bit larger in size. I thought it could be Adie’s pupil that's why he is asking for slit lamp examination to look for vermiform movements But honestly there was no such thing... ant segment was perfectly fine, examiner asked to quickly see the fundus: Bilateral large discs with healthy NRR, CDR almost 0.8 Ou. Descirbed the disc findings and the bell rang. While leaving the room he showed me the OCT ONH and asked does this patient have glaucoma? I quickly had a look at OCT printout and made sure that the cup was symmetrical in size and there was no RNFL loss and quickly responded as per clinical exam findings and OCT printout that there was no sign of glaucoma. No comments from the examiner as he was expressionless again but i had seen him marking tick on the fail side column 😜 This case gave me nightmares till the result date. Honestly i might have missed some findings..

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25-4-24) - Oculoplasty Cases
sections.content:
Case-1. Young girl sitting on chair with right eye mild ptosis and 15 degree exotropia and bilateral congested looking eyes. Command was to inspect and tell findings , Then do the right eye ptosis measurements, did all parameters like VA(NPL in right eye) pupil examination (eccentric pupil) pseudophakic right eye, MRD1, PFH, LF,-and at the end checked the bell’s phenomenon which was really poor in both eyes.. I wanted to check EOM but examiner refused & said no need. Question was what would you do for this patient? I replied i would like to take history and examine the patient on slit lamp and counsel the patient and would observe and consider conservative treatment options as the patient had poor bell’s phenomenon. Would you do surgery? I said NO.

Case-2: Old lady with left eye cicatricial ectropion with chemical injury on left side of the face. Described the findings while examining the patient, palpated the scar and lid laxity tests as there was also horizontal lid laxity present then I asked to see the patient on a slit lamp as well. Told the Management options as usual written in the books.. Ok now examine the other eye of the same lady, there was right eye sebaceous cyst below the superotemporal orbital margin, did all methods of cyst examination. What are your differentials and management? Told excision biopsy and histopathological examination afterwards.

Case-3) Slit lamp examination of left eye of young male. I could only describe the findings in the given time which were; Lower lid trichiasis touching the globe with symblepharon obscuring the lower punctum +Bulbar congestion and corneal scarring, Lid margin was normal no entropion noted. & The bell rang. Alhamdulillah Oculoplasty station was sastisfactory as i managed to see one extra case.

sections.title: Clinical Examination (25-4-24) - Anterior Segment Cases
sections.content:
Case-1: Young girl around 15 years old sitting on slit lamp. Command was to examine the anterior segment of left eye: It was a case of CAU with band keratopathy, could be JRA. Findings were: Pseudophakic , seclusio pupilae, iris bombe, KPs, AC cells +1, peripheral iridocorneal touch 360 degree. Questions were Differentials, Causes of band keratopathy in non inflammatory conditions other than ocular causes.

Case-2. Young male on slit lamp. Command was to examine the anterior segment of left eye then right eye.. Left eye: failed keratoplasty graft e very hazy view of the AC with superficial and deep vascularization and anterior stamphyloma at 6 O’clock away from graft host junction. Some sutures were also removed. I was asked is the patient phakic or aphakic? I replied i cant comment bcz there is no view-he smiled and said fair enough. OK examine the right eye: It was perfectly fine normal Clear cornea: quiet ac No sign of keratoconus. He asked is there any sign of keratoconus i said as per my examination of anterior segment there is no sign of keratoconus. He agreed. Ok what are the tests to check for keratoconus? I replied refraction with K values and corneal topography. Is the graft in left eye failed or is there a graft rejection? It was a tricky question.. I said sir graft rejection is One of the reasons of graft failure but i would like to take the history n would like to know the time of surgery done to check for primary graft failure or late graft failure. I guess he understood i knew the concept. Ok last question, what would you do for corneal vascularisation? I said i can do cauterization and sub-conj/intrastromal anti vegfs in addition to topical steroids.. He smiled and replied im happy and patted on my back you can leave and then the bell rang. The clinical exam was over and i was still skeptical whether i would pass or not due to the neuro case till the result day… Finally on 23rd May result was publised on my dashboard that dr dont worry you are now a fellow of RCPS glasgow. 😀 ALHAMDULILLAH! The home tip is to believe in yourself and control your nerves -don’t worry about anyone bad case during the exam as still, you can get through by achieving additional marks elsewhere they judge your overall clinical skills. Behave like a fellow and do the usual examination as you do in your routine opd practice. Regarding OSCE, they can ask anything so your theory must be super strong. 💪 Wish you all the best Regards 🙏 Dr Muhammad Ahsen. FRCS (glasgow), FCPS (Pak) If any queries u can contact me at this email: dr.ahsen9999@gmail.com

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's FRCS Experience (Amman, April 2024)
sections.content: My Name Is Amr Mohamed, I am a pediatric ophthalmologist from Yemen. I passed the exam on the first attempt Alhamdulillah after a preparation of 2 months (3 weeks of vacation before the exam to fully concentrate on preparation).

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Study Sources
content: 1. Kanski 8th edition.
2. Practical Guide to VIVA and OSCE in Ophthalmology Examinations (Wong).
3. Internal medicine notes (Dr. Waleed Badr).

4. Previous Exam experiences (2015-2023), the most valuable source, you need to study previous exam experiences and answer the questions, you will find a pattern and favorite questions, and stick to that, 80% of the exam will come from it.

5. Having A study partner, and 1 hour of daily practice, each participant will prepare 3 questions (from past candidates’ experiences with answers) and we will ask each other, I would like to thank my friends whom I studied with Dr. Mehmet from Turkey Dr. Ahmed from Egypt and other colleagues.
6. Clinical examination videos (Dr. Ayman Al Ghoneimy and Dr. Mohammed El Naggar). Check Dr. El Naggar’s Videos on YouTube (Arabic narration).
7. Dr. Ghada Zein El-Abedin's channel has a lot of valuable resources along with other exam experiences on YouTube.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Viva Examination (23/4/2024) - Station 1: General Medicine & Neurology
sections.content:
1. (written scenario) asked me about the history of a patient undergoing cataract surgery who was found to have atrial fibrillation. What will you do? I told him that the patient I needed to know whether it was acute atrial fibrillation or chronic and the patient would need beta blockers like Esmolol, in addition to Digoxin, and if no improvement the patient would need cardioversion whether electric cardioversion or drug cardioversion with amiodarone and also patient need anticoagulant like warfarin. The examiner asked me what other drugs were for anticoagulation. He asked me about the causes of atrial fibrillation.

2. (written scenario) You Have a patient who has a cataract and plans to do cataract surgery and he is on warfarin. What will you do? I told him that we can plan the surgery under topical anesthesia or subtenon anesthesia to avoid risk of retrobulbar hemorrhages and we can do clear corneal incision. I don't know if he wants something else, but he did not comment at all. I would coordinate with the physician whether we can stop warfarin or give another anticoagulant.

3. (written scenario) Female with the Galactorrhea and Amenorrhea, what is the diagnosis? I told him that the patient is having chiasmatic lesion mostly pituitary adenoma. Then he said what are you going to do (examination and investigations)? I told him anterior segment, posterior segment, check the optic disc, check the pupillary reaction and check the confrontation visual field and visual field test (automated perimetry). We need to do a neuroimaging, brain MRI and hormonal essay for the prolactin and other pituitary hormones. Then, I asked about expected visual field defect? I told him that Bitemporal hemianopia usually starting with the superior field. Then he asked me what drugs can you give for this patient? I told him bromocriptine or cabergoline. Then he said other options? I told if the patient is still having complaints or there is progressive visual field loss, then we can proceed for surgery. Then he said what is the surgery? I told transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, he said Any other options? I stereotactic radiotherapy. I think he wanted something else, but I didn't know. Then he said post-surgery the patient developed polyuria. What is the problem? I couldn’t answer properly.

4. A case scenario of a patient with diplopia and ptosis (I forgot the main scenario) but the questions were about myasthenia gravis, the clinical tests and the pharmacological tests, tensilon test specifically in details.

5. (written scenario) a case of five-year-old patient child with vision 6/6 and 6/18. what are you going to do? I told him. Anterior segment, posterior segment, cover tests, extraocular motility, cycloplegic refraction, The Examiner said everything is normal. Then I told him it could be amblyopia, then examiner asked what is amblyopia and what are the types of amblyopia and what are you going to do? I told him I will give glasses if any significant refractive error or anisometropia, and amblyopia therapy, he asked would you do amblyopia therapy immediately? Then asked about Amblyopia therapy modalities? I told him patching of the good eye, four to five hours. He said that the patient's five-year-old would you start the patching directly, I said yes immediately. he said OK, what are the other options? I told him atropine drops. what is that called? I said penalization.

6. (written scenario) patient three-year old with acute onset of convergent strabismus for one month, he told me what are the differential diagnoses? I told him acute esotropia and accommodative esotropia. What else? 6 the cranial nerve palsy. what are you going to do? I mentioned full examination including cover tests, extraocular motility to differentiate whether it is concomitant or incomitant, pupillary reflexes, anterior segment and posterior segment, cycloplegic refraction, he said. What is the most common cause in this age group? I told accommodative ET, what are you going to do for this? I told him full cycloplegic hypermetropic refraction glasses and treat amblyopia If there is any fixation preference.

7. (written scenario) it was elderly patient with lateral rectus paralysis, what are you going to do? I said I will ask history about any systemic diseases and history of the onset, progression and the duration, measuring the angle and checking the other cranial nerve, anterior & posterior segment examinations, pupillary examination. Then he said what are the investigations would you do? I told him about investigations such as blood sugar and lipid profile, neuroimaging also, how would you manage? I told we can do patching of one of the eyes or prism glasses, He said OK The patient came after six months with the same deviation. I told him if deviation is stable, we can proceed with strabismus surgery, he said. What else? I told him botulinum toxin but usually after six months, it is not effective because of medial rectus restriction. And he said what else? I told Fresnel prisms.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Viva Examination (23/4/2024) - Station 2: Anterior Segment & Oculoplasty
sections.content:
1. (written scenario) patient who will do a cataract surgery under local anesthesia. What are the historical points That is important? I told some of them like systemic diseases. Then I asked about the onset, progression, duration of the cataract. Any pain? Any other complaints? Anterior segment, Posterior segment? Intraocular pressure, Check the other eye, ask about history of trauma, check the pupils, check the extraocular motility. He kept saying what else, what else? I think there is one table in Kansky (lens chapter) that have a lot of things regarding preoperative assessment (respiratory disease, rheumatoid arthritis, etc. Then he asked about the examination. I told him also that during the evaluation I want to evaluate whether the patients fit for local anesthesia or not. because in some cases like patients with parkinsonism or seizures it is not possible.

2. a photograph of a child with left leukocoria. He said, what is this? I told him left leukocoria and told him the differential diagnosis. Then he said, OK, if this is PHPV, what are you going to do? I said it depends whether it is anterior PHPV or posterior PHPV. If Anterior PHPV we can do cataract surgery with a guarded visual prognosis said, what are you going to counsel the patient’s family about? I told him about visual prognosis and need of amblyopia therapy post operatively and risk of glaucoma, retinal detachment. I mentioned also approach to a case of leukocoria regarding EUA and B scan ultrasonography.

3. How would you counsel a patient for cataract surgery? I will tell the patient there is a risk of PCR, not putting IOL, Risk of endophthalmitis, bullous keratopathy, glaucoma, and persistent uveitis. Risk of rupture group or retrobulbar hemorrhage from anesthesia.

4. The examiner handed me a photo of lower lid basal cell carcinoma. It was rodent ulcer So asking me to describe? what is the most probable diagnosis, how would you treat and details about the reconstruction?

5. A question about dry eye disease. Slit lamp photo of a patient with rose Bengal stain, asked describe and what other stains that can be used? And what is another test of dry eye? I mentioned tear break up time. Schirmer test 1 &2. tear meniscus height. Then asked how would you treat this patient? I told if there is any systemic disease we need to treat the underlying cause. Then we can start with environmental changes with lid hygiene, frequent blinking, and goggles. Then I talked about artificial tears. If no improvement, we can shift to preservative-free artificial tears with topical steroid and cyclosporin. I told him also about punctual plugs, he said, what is the systemic treatment that can be given. I told him doxycycline for meibomian gland dysfunction but I think he wanted also other things. Then I said we can do surgeries if the patient is having any disease like entropion or trichiasis or ectropion.

6. Then he gave a photo of an elderly female closing her eyes forcefully and there was left lagophthalmos, he asked what it is and what is the most probable diagnosis. Told there is lagophthalmos and most probably there is facial nerve palsy because there was also mouth deviation. And then he said, OK, what are you going to do? I said refer to neurologist Then for the eye temporary measures we can give lubricant eyedrops, lubricant ointments, eyelid tapping. Then if it is permanent facial nerve palsy like compressing lesion or permanent damage of the nerve then we can do permanent measures, He said What are those measures? I told medial canthoplasty, lateral tarsorrhaphy, gold weight implant. Then he said do you do those procedures by yourself? I said no, and he also told me what about botulinum toxin? I said yes, we can give botulinum toxin and he said in those patients usually what they have tearing or dryness, I said tearing. He said why? I said because of punctal eversion and reflex tearing. He then said if you are not doing those surgeries by yourself, what are you going to do? I said I would refer patient to oculoplastic surgeon? He said OK

7. (case scenario) a case of a child with lid swelling and redness for two days. I answered it might be preseptal cellulitis, orbital cellulitis or conjunctivitis. Then asked how to differentiate orbital from preseptal cellulitis? then next question was if it is a case of orbital cellulitis what are you going to do? I told him admission, CBC to check WBC's temperature, ENT consultation, CT orbit & sinuses to check if there is a subperiosteal Abscess and to differentiate whether it's preseptal or orbital. Also, clinical signs of orbital cellulitis like proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, optic nerve affection, and pupils.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Viva Examination (23/4/2024) - Station 3: Posterior Segment & Glaucoma
sections.content:
1. He asked are you doing trabeculectomy? I said no, but I observed a trab before. He said OK if you did trab and post op day One, patient has AC shallow and IOP 3 mm Hg. What are you going to do? I said I need to assess first the degree of AC shallowness whether it is grade 1,2,3 whether it is iridocorneal or pupillo-corneal or lenticulo-corneal. Then I need to check seidel test whether positive or negative, assess bleb height, Differential it might be over filtration or bleb leak or ciliary shutdown. Then I said also I need to check the fundus. Then he said could it be a choroidal detachment? I said yes, it could be choroidal detachment. Then asked what are you going to do? I said that we can give bandage contact lens but he said bandage contact lens will not be enough and it will not sit properly. I said, OK, we can do patching he said. What else? I said we can decrease the steroid, increase the antibiotic eye drops, Said OK, what else? Then I did a mistake. I said we can do drainage for the choroidal detachment; he was not happy with that.

2. Then he asked me another scenario, if the patient also with trabeculectomy and post operatively, he has a pressure 70 mm Hg. I said, OK, we have 3 possibilities whether 1. pupillary block and it can be checked with transillumination, 2. suprachoroidal hemorrhage and it can be checked with B scan or from examination. And the third possibility is malignant glaucoma or aqueous misdirection said, OK, it’s is malignant glaucoma. What are you going to do? I said cycloplegic eye drops, he said Did you see malignant glaucoma this before? I said yes, he said. Do they benefit from cycloplegic eyedrops? I said mostly no, but it can help some of the patients. I forgot actually to mention antiglaucoma groups. Then he said, what else? I said if the patient is pseudophakic, yag laser posterior capsulotomy and hyaloidotomy can be done. And if the patient is phakic, we can also do YAG laser through PI. Otherwise, I would refer the patient to VR surgeon, to do vitrectomy.

3. A patient with primary open angle glaucoma. For example, patient is having IOP 30 mm Hg. What are you going to give him? I told him we can start him with the one antiglaucoma eye drops Whether beta blocker if There are no contraindications like Timolol 0.5% twice daily or we can give prostaglandin analogues Latanoprost, Travoprost or Bimatoprost once daily at bed time. He said OKAY after giving your patient prostaglandin analogues and What are you going to tell him? I said about the complications. Like red eye, trichomegaly, Iris hyperpigmentation and I told him about counselling the patient that he needed to know that he needed to comply to this eye drops for the rest of the life because it is a progressive and chronic disease. He said OK patient was not comfortable. Then I said I can shift to another antiglaucoma. He said OK patient is not tolerant to any anti glaucoma eye drops. I said we can do laser trabeculoplasty said he don't want laser. Then I said preservative free anti glaucoma and that was the answer he was looking for.

4. Fourth question: a photo of a patient with the central retinal artery occlusion with cilioretinal artery sparing, he said What are you going to do? I said about the emergency treatment, breathing in a paper bag, carbogen, antiglaucoma, ocular massage, paracentesis, also checking the other eye and referring the patient urgently to internist to do investigations like Carotid Doppler ultrasound and echocardiogram.

5. The examiner asked about VMT case (OCT Macula picture) what is the treatment? I said it depends on the vision and the visual symptoms. If the patient has good vision and no metamorphopsia then we can observe the patient because some of the cases will improve spontaneously. If the vision is worsening or there is a severe metamorphosis, then we can do pars plana vitrectomy with membrane removal and sometimes with ILM peeling. The examiner stopped here.

6. a patient having rheumatoid arthritis and he's taking systemic medications. What are the drugs that can affect the eye? I said about the steroids causing posterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma and increase the risk of infections. Then I talked about hydroxychloroquine and she asked about Bull’s eye maculopathy and how to diagnose? how to screen the patient? Patient evaluation? what is the toxic dose and what are the condition that if the patient is having risk of drug toxicity will increase. It was renal disease, but I couldn't answer that.

7. A photo of glaucomatous optic disk. It was a large disk with large vertical cupping with peripapillary atrophy, nasalization of the optic disc and bayonetting. Then examiner said what are you going to do for this patient? I said full evaluation of the glaucoma. She stressed on the role of the central corneal thickness and the importance. I talked about underestimation and what is the normal corneal thickness, investigations like visual field, OCT nerve fiber layer.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Clinical Examination (25/4/2024) - Station 1: Oculoplasty
sections.content:
1. A 45-year-old Female with bilateral dermatochalasis and ptosis. Examiner Just said EXAMINE, I started by observation I can see bilateral ptosis and dermatochalasis. He said OK. I said I want to examine ptosis. He said proceed. So, I did the MRD1 It was -1 in right eye and 2mm in the left eye. Then Palpebral fissure height height, then Levator function and Lid crease. Then I told him I want to check lagophthalmos. I did it. Then Bell's phenomena. Then I told him corneal sensation. Then I told him I want to check for the cause. I told him I want to do fatigability test. He said how? I said I will let the patient to look up for 30 seconds then I will repeat the measurements of ptosis. Also, I can do ice test or sleep test. He said what are investigations that can be done? I said acetylcholine receptor antibodies and EMG single fiber and edrophonium test or neostigmine test. what is the result in single fiber EMG? I could not answer. Then asked how will you treat myasthenia gravis? I told him patient will need pyridostigmine and oral steroids in some cases and I would refer the patient to a neurologist for further evaluation and management.

2. Examiner asked me to examine patient’s right eye using slit lamp. I checked the eye there was an ACIOL with deep AC, clear cornea. I told the findings. Then I stopped examination. Then he told me this is oculoplastic session, please look again at the eye. When I looked again, I looked at the lids and I found I found DCR tube. Asked what are the indications for DCR and what are the complications of DCR.

3. Third case was a young male patient with right eye Phthisis Bulbi. He told me examine with the torch and he told me what is this? I told Phthisis Bulbi. He said why that can happen. I told the chronic endophthalmitis post intraocular surgery or severe trauma. He said OK look again and check what is the cause. I checked again I could not answer what is the specific cause for the case. Then he told me OK what are you going to do for him? I told him for Cosmesis we can give colored contact lenses or prosthetic shell or because of the loss of orbital volume, we can go for evisceration with orbital implant and prosthetic shell. Time UP.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Clinical Examination (25/4/2024) - Station 2: Anterior Segment
sections.content:
1. Examine Left eye. clear cornea and two sutures and irregular pupil with a slightly inferiorly subluxated scleral fixation IOL. AC reaction +1. The examiner asked what could happen to the patient? I told maybe a traumatic cataract and there was no capsular support or maybe the patient was pseudophakic and IOL dislocated, then second surgery done or third scenario that it might be a primary aphakia and secondary scleral fixation IOL because there is no support. He said, OK, what are the things that you want to examine? I said intraocular pressure and fundus. He said why intraocular pressure? I said that the patient might have a glaucoma from the main cause of the trauma. If it is a traumatic case maybe like cyclodialysis or angle recession He said what else I couldn't answer. He said you mentioned there is AC reaction. I answered it might be uveitic glaucoma. Then asked for IOL subluxation what are you going to do? I said I will check the vision. If vision is good then only conservatively managed with glasses. If vision is bad then patient might need contact lenses or refractive surgery.

2. An elderly patient with pseudophakic bullous keratopathy. He had a large superior corneal wound. Maybe intra capsular or extra capsular cataract extraction. There was a large part of iris loss superiorly from 8:00 to 2:00 and patient had pseudophakic bullous keratopathy with a central epithelial defect. I mentioned the findings. He said what could happen to the patient. I said maybe intra capsular cataract extraction complicated or extra capsular cataract extraction complicated without IOL. Then Asked what are you going to do for the patient? I said if IOP and B scan is normal then we can proceed for graft. He said what type of graft? I said whether penetrating keratoplasty or endothelial keratoplasty, depending on the level of stromal scarring, if it is full thickness then we will need penetrating keratoplasty. Then he said, OK, what else? I said also IOL implantation. I told him whether we do staged procedure, graft first, then IOL or a Combined procedure. he asked meabout the advantages of each procedure. I told him then he said OK if you did not put IOL only graft what can be done? I couldn’t answer. he said OK you can use contact lens for correction rather than doing second surgery.

3. Examiner said just give me the diagnosis. I told patient has endothelial keratoplasty and pseudophakic. He told me OK, what do you think is this graft clear? I said clear but he said Are you sure? Check again. I could not answer properly this question.

He said what is the grading of the macular hole and what are the causes of macular hole and what is the surgery for macular hole and what are the complications of gas injection and what are the types of gases and what are the precautions that you will give to the patient post gas injection? He said OK, I mentioned also that the patient is pseudophakic. Examiner asked what are the indications for vitrectomy in diabetes? I told persistent vitreous hemorrhage or tractional detachment threatening the macula or combined retinal tractional detachment with rhegmatogenous detachment. He said, OK, this patient is vitrectomized. Did you see silicone? I said no, I could not see silicone. He said OK, what are the complications of silicon oil in vitrectomy? Then I said glaucoma, band keratopathy. Then asked about for how long you should keep the silicone? I said ideally between three and six months but sometimes we need longer tamponade in some cases. Then the other examiner asked me about PRP laser, how to do PRP laser. Then Itold him the settings and how many spots. Then asked about macular edema. If the patient is having macular edema, I told I need to give intravitreal injection. He said what are the types of intravitreal injection? I told Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab and aflibercept. Then the other examiner told me if the patient is having macular edema and vitreomacular traction, what can you do? I said the intravitreal injections is contraindicated. laser might increase traction as well , then we can do vitrectomy to remove the membrane and to improve the macular edema.

3. Examine with 90D this child (8 OR 9 year-old- boy) . He told me spot diagnosis? The disc was really very strange. I didn't reach the diagnosis. I told maybe it is a congenital optic disc anomaly might be morning glory or optic disc coloboma or glaucomatous optic disc. Time UP

He said OK so I did the cover tests at near and at distance patient has alternating exotropia. Then I said I want to measure the deviation. He said OK go ahead. He gave me prism bar and I did measurement for the deviation. It was 35 prism diopter exotropia. Then he asked me do you want to measure deviation without glasses. I told him OK. Then I asked the patient can you see without glasses. He said I cannot see. Then I just did Hirschberg and I told him almost the same angle. Then I checked the motility. Patient had inferior oblique overaction in both eyes. Then he told me what are you going to do? I said I will do full examination including anterior & posterior segment, give glasses and treat amblyopia if present then check then I will do surgery.

2. Middle Aged woman, examine pupils I checked for heterochromia and anisocoria in light, then asked to switch off the light and checked anisocoria in dark. Then I checked direct and consensual light reflexes and swinging flash light test. I noticed Grade 1 RAPD in the left eye from the second attempt. Then examiner asked what you want to do? I told I want to check the fundus. He said OK check it. I checked patient had the cupped disc and disc and pallor. I told him it might be glaucomatous optic neuropathy. He said check the other eye. other eye disc was normal. Then he told me what it could be. I could not answer properly. He asked me what are the types of optic atrophy. I told him primary, secondary and consecutive optic atrophy. Then he told me this is which one. I could not answer properly his questions.

3. Then Examiner asked me to perform confrontation visual field test for a third patient. I just started with the beginning of the visual field. Then the bell rang and I could not complete the case.

sections.title: Dr. Amr Mohamed's Post-Exam Comments & Advice
content: 1. There is a grading system to evaluate candidate performance. You don’t need to answer every question to pass.

2. My single best advice is to keep calm during exam, it is a mind game as many past candidates said. One of my colleagues advised me to forget that you are in an exam and take it as a discussion with a senior colleague.
3. If you didn’t perform well in one station, keep fighting you still have the chance to pass if you perform well in other stations.
4. Practice clinical examination and master the techniques before the exam, just keep repeating again and again to master it.
5. Keep praying and prepare well and you will pass in sha Allah.
6. Definitely examiners are helpful, some examiners are not very helpful but I believe the examination system is fair and no one can fail you unless you perform poorly.

7. Do a lot of oral and clinical simulated exams, that’s the best way to be mentally and psychologically prepared. Sometimes you know a lot of information but you don’t know how to express it, simulated exams with study partners will help.
Feel Free to contact if I can help in anyway, All the best for all the candidates, definitely it is a tough journey but it is worth it.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Papilloma Differentials
Clinical Pearl: Post-Phaco Refractive Error
content: Early Management: Rule out corneal edema, wound integrity, IOL position. Optimize tear film.
Late Management: Biometry review, IOL power calculation error (most common), IOL malposition (tilt, decentration), astigmatism (pre-existing, surgically induced), dry eye, pseudo-accommodation.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Phenomenon
content: Congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis.
Characterized by retraction and elevation of the ptotic eyelid upon stimulation of the ipsilateral pterygoid muscles (e.g., chewing, sucking, jaw movement).

Management depends on severity: Observation, amblyopia treatment, ptosis surgery (levator resection for mild-moderate ptosis, bilateral levator excision with frontalis suspension for severe ptosis with prominent winking).

sections.title: Red Flag: Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR) during Phacoemulsification
content: Immediate recognition is crucial to minimize complications.
Signs: Sudden deepening of AC, momentary pupillary dilation, posterior movement of lens fragments, vitreous presence.

Management steps: Stop phaco, inject viscoelastic, check for vitreous, perform anterior vitrectomy (if vitreous prolapse), consider IOL options (ACIOL, iris-fixated, scleral-fixated, or aphakia with contact lens/glasses).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Corneal Dystrophies (Lattice-like)

rows: Amyloid deposits, refractile lattice lines, recurrent erosions, reduced vision
Hyaline deposits, discrete white 'bread crumb' opacities, RCE less common than LCD1
Mucopolysaccharide deposits, diffuse stromal haze + gray-white opacities, vision severely affected, RCE rare
Systemic amyloidosis, facial nerve palsy, skin laxity. Ocular: lattice lines (peripheral), prominent RCE less common

sections.title: Red Flag: Ocular Trauma - Ruptured Globe/IOFB
content: Suspect ruptured globe with any high-velocity injury or penetrating trauma.
Symptoms: Pain, blurred vision, lid swelling, subconjunctival hemorrhage (360 degrees, chemosis, 'donut' pattern), hyphema, irregular pupil, shallow AC, soft eye.
Management: IMMEDIATE eye shield (no pressure), NPO, antiemetics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, urgent surgical repair.
Corneo-scleral tear repair: First suture at the limbus (corneal side first). Use 10-0 nylon for cornea, 8-0 or 7-0 vicryl for sclera. Explore posterior extent of tear if needed.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Post-Trabeculectomy Complications
content: Early: Hyphema, shallow AC, hypotony (overfiltration, bleb leak, ciliary shutdown), choroidal detachment, malignant glaucoma, wound leak, infection.
Late: Bleb fibrosis/failure, bleb leak, bleb infection/endophthalmitis, late-onset hypotony, cataract progression.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Thin/Avascular Bleb
Management Protocol: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG)
content: Step 1: Treat underlying cause (e.g., PRP for ischemic CRVO/DR, anti-VEGF for rapid regression of neovascularization).
Step 2: Control IOP (topical anti-glaucoma meds - avoid miotics if rubeosis present, oral acetazolamide).
Step 3: Reduce inflammation (topical steroids).
Step 4: Surgical intervention if medical/laser fails: Glaucoma drainage devices (e.g., Ahmed valve) or cyclophotocoagulation (for eyes with poor visual potential).

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) Interpretation
content: Reliability Indices: Fixation Losses (<20% good), False Positives (<15% good), False Negatives (<15% good).
Testing Algorithms: SITA Standard (reliable, good for baseline), SITA Fast (quicker, less reliable for subtle defects), SITA Faster (even quicker, useful for follow-up).

sections.title: Management Protocol: BRVO & Macular Edema
content: 1. Confirm diagnosis: Fundus exam, fluorescein angiography (FA), OCT (for macular edema).
2. Systemic workup: Identify and manage systemic risk factors (HTN, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, coagulopathies, glaucoma). Referral to internist/cardiologist.
3. Macular Edema (CME) Management: Anti-VEGF injections (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, Bevacizumab) are first-line. Steroid implants (Dexamethasone, Fluocinolone) are alternatives.
4. Neovascularization (NV) Management: If retinal ischemia leads to neovascularization, laser photocoagulation (grid laser or scatter laser) may be needed.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Metamorphopsia & Blurred Vision in Elderly
Management Protocol: Macular Hole
content: Diagnosis: OCT is key for confirmation and staging (Stage I-IV).
Stage 1 (Foveal cyst/split, impending hole): Observation, sometimes jet vitrectomy if progressive.
Stage 2-4 (Full-thickness): Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling and gas tamponade (e.g., SF6, C2F6, C3F8).
Post-operative: Face-down positioning (critical for hole closure), avoid air travel.
Complications: Cataract, retinal detachment, glaucoma, endophthalmitis, gas migration.

sections.title: Investigation Workup: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP)
content: Electrophysiology: ERG (reduced/extinguished rod and cone responses).
Visual Field: Peripheral constriction (tubular vision).
OCT: Macular edema, atrophy, epiretinal membrane.
Autofluorescence: RPE atrophy pattern.
Genetic testing: Identify causative gene mutations (e.g., RHO, USH2A, RPGR).

sections.title: Graves' Ophthalmopathy: Pathophysiology & Management
sections.content:
Pathophysiology: Autoimmune disorder where antibodies (TRAb) stimulate TSH receptors on orbital fibroblasts, leading to increased GAG production, fat accumulation, and inflammation of extraocular muscles (EOMs) and orbital fat. This causes muscle swelling, proptosis, and restricted eye movements.

Systemic Signs (other than ocular): Thyroid gland enlargement (goiter), hyperthyroidism symptoms (tachycardia, weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance), pretibial myxedema (skin thickening on shins), thyroid acropachy (clubbing of fingers/toes).

Treatment Options: Depends on severity and activity (CAS score). Lubricants for dry eye, prisms for diplopia, orbital decompression (for optic neuropathy or severe proptosis), strabismus surgery (for stable diplopia), eyelid surgery (for lid retraction). Systemic: high-dose steroids (IV preferred for active disease), orbital radiotherapy, teprotumumab (new targeted therapy).

sections.title: Red Flag: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) with Papilledema
content: Hallmark: Papilledema, often bilateral, due to elevated CSF pressure. Can lead to irreversible vision loss.
Investigations: Neuroimaging (MRI brain with venography to rule out structural causes/CVT), Lumbar Puncture (elevated opening pressure >25 cm H2O in adults, normal CSF composition).

Management: Weight loss (crucial), Acetazolamide (first-line), close monitoring of vision/fields/papilledema. Surgical options for progressive vision loss despite maximal medical therapy: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) or CSF shunting (VP or LP shunt). Referral to neurology and neurosurgeon is essential.

branches: Structural Brain Lesions (tumors, stroke, trauma, malformations)

branches.label: Management
branches: Acute: Protect patient from injury, position on side, administer benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam IV) if prolonged.
Long-term: Antiepileptic drugs, address underlying cause.

branches.label: Ophthalmic Relevance
branches: Drug-induced ocular side effects (e.g., phenytoin toxicity, topiramate glaucoma)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Swollen Optic Disc with Pain on Eye Movements

rows: Unilateral vision loss (acute), dyschromatopsia, afferent pupillary defect
Often associated with MS (MRI brain for plaques)
Sudden, painless vision loss (altitudinal defect), disc edema (pallid or hyperemic)
Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is critical DDx (ESR/CRP, temporal artery biopsy)
Severe, bilateral optic neuritis, often recurrent, spinal cord involvement
Variable vision loss, disc edema, vitreous cells
Syphilis, Lyme disease, viral infections (e.g., VZV)
Systemic inflammatory signs, chest imaging, serum ACE
Slow, progressive vision loss, mild edema (early), later atrophy

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Unilateral Ptosis with Double Vision and Headache (3rd Nerve vs. Horner's)

rows: Severe (complete eyelid closure), often with eyelid retraction on attempted upgaze
Mild (1-2mm), often with inverse ptosis (lower lid elevation)
Dilated (mydriasis), often fixed to light if pupil-involving
Constricted (miosis), anisocoria worse in dark, reacts to light
Limitation of adduction, elevation, depression (down-and-out position)
Common (especially with compressive lesions like aneurysm)
Variable, can be associated with pain (e.g., carotid dissection)
Absent Bell's phenomenon, potential for aberrant regeneration

sections.title: Management Protocol: Intermittent Exotropia
content: 1. Initial Assessment: Confirm diagnosis, measure deviation (distance/near, with/without correction), assess fusion, stereoacuity, amblyopia, convergence.
2. Refractive Correction: Prescribe full refractive correction, especially hyperopia/astigmatism. Correct any anisometropia.
3. Amblyopia Treatment: Patching or atropine penalization if present.
4. Non-Surgical Options: Observation (if well-controlled), prismatic correction (temporary for diplopia, rarely for long-term), orthoptic exercises (convergence insufficiency type).

5. Surgical Management: Indicated if control worsens, deviation increases, or symptoms (diplopia, asthenopia, cosmetic concern) persist despite conservative measures. Recess lateral rectus muscles (uni- or bilateral) or resect medial rectus (often combined). Consider adjustable sutures in adults.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Complications of Silicone Oil (IOFB/RRD cases)
content: Glaucoma (most common, due to inflammation, pupillary block, silicone oil migration)
Cataract (nuclear sclerosis, often rapid progression)
Band keratopathy (due to silicone oil emulsification)
Corneal edema/decompensation (if oil emulsifies into AC)
Retinal redetachment after oil removal
Diplopia, phthisis bulbi (rare)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Infantile Esotropia

branches: Sixth Nerve Palsy (rare in infancy, usually incomitant)

Sensory Esotropia (due to poor vision in one eye)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Anisocoria & Large Discs

content.center: Anisocoria (larger pupil in dark) & Large Discs

branches.label: Anisocoria (worse in dark - impaired sympathetic)
branches: Physiological Anisocoria (rarely more noticeable in dark)

branches.label: Large Optic Discs (often with large C/D ratio)
branches: Myopic Optic Neuropathy (myopic tilt, temporal crescent)
Glaucoma (progressive thinning of NRR, asymmetry, hemorrhage, RNFL defects)
Combined Presentation: May suggest a complex neuro-ophthalmic or structural issue requiring comprehensive evaluation (e.g., prior trauma, congenital anomalies affecting both).
