rows: Unilateral/bilateral, present at birth, poor LF, possible amblyopia
Variable, fatigable, worse late day, often bilateral asymmetric
Diplopia, orbicularis weakness (Bell's poor), generalized weakness
High lid crease, thin lid skin
Due to lid mass, scar, edema

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Sebaceous Cyst (Eyelid)

branches: Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (must rule out for sebaceous lesions, biopsy is crucial)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Trichiasis & Symblepharon
content: Trichiasis: Epilation (temporary), Electrolysis, Cryotherapy, Argon Laser, Surgical excision with lid margin reconstruction.
Symblepharon: Prevention (early management of chemical burns with symblepharon rings/AMT), Surgical lysis with conjunctival graft/AMT, Amniotic membrane transplantation.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Chronic Anterior Uveitis (CAU) with Band Keratopathy

branches: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) / Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (JRA)
Herpetic Uveitis (less common to cause BK)
Metabolic Causes of Band Keratopathy (non-inflammatory, non-ocular): Hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity), chronic renal failure, gout, chronic mercury exposure.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Failed Keratoplasty Graft & Corneal Vascularization
content: 1. Confirm Graft Failure: Rule out rejection (epithelial, stromal, endothelial), infection, persistent inflammation, recurrent disease, chronic endothelial decompensation.
2. History: Time of surgery (primary vs. late graft failure), previous rejections, underlying corneal pathology.

3. Management of Graft Failure: Depends on cause. For rejection, intensive topical/systemic steroids. For infection, appropriate antimicrobials. For endothelial failure, repeat keratoplasty (PKP, DMEK, DSAEK).

4. Corneal Vascularization Treatment: Topical steroids (to suppress inflammation), Anti-VEGF (subconjunctival, intrastromal, topical - off-label), Laser photocoagulation (argon laser to feeder vessels), Cauterization of feeder vessels (intraoperative or transconjunctival).

sections.title: Perioperative Management: Atrial Fibrillation for Cataract Surgery
content: Determine if acute vs. chronic AF.
Rate Control: Beta-blockers (e.g., Esmolol), calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem), digoxin.
Rhythm Control: Antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g., amiodarone), cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological) if unstable or recent onset.
Anticoagulation: Warfarin, DOACs (direct oral anticoagulants like rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban). CHADS2-VASc score guides long-term anticoagulation.
Coordination: Consult with cardiologist/internist for optimization before surgery.
Red Flag: Uncontrolled AF increases risk of stroke and myocardial infarction perioperatively. Postpone elective surgery until stable.

sections.title: Perioperative Management: Cataract Surgery on Warfarin
content: Risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage with regional anesthesia (retrobulbar, peribulbar block).
Anesthesia Options: Topical anesthesia, subconjunctival, or subtenon anesthesia (with careful technique) are safer choices.
Surgical Approach: Clear corneal incision is preferred over scleral tunnel incisions to minimize bleeding.

Anticoagulation Management: Generally, for routine cataract surgery, warfarin does not need to be stopped if INR is in therapeutic range (e.g., 2.0-3.0). Discontinuation carries higher thrombotic risk than bleeding risk in this context.
Bridging therapy is usually NOT recommended for cataract surgery. Always consult with the prescribing physician/hematologist to assess individual thrombotic risk vs. bleeding risk.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Galactorrhea & Amenorrhea
Investigation & Management: Pituitary Adenoma (Prolactinoma)
sections.content:
Examination: Anterior segment, posterior segment (optic disc), pupillary reaction, confrontation visual field, automated perimetry (for bitemporal hemianopia, usually starting superiorly).

Neuroimaging: Brain MRI with pituitary protocol is essential.

Hormonal Assay: Prolactin level (significantly elevated), other pituitary hormones (TSH, free T4, cortisol, GH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone).

Medical Treatment: Dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine, Cabergoline) are first-line for prolactinomas, often normalizing prolactin and reducing tumor size.

Surgical Treatment: Transsphenoidal hypophysectomy for progressive visual field loss, macroadenomas unresponsive to medical therapy, or apoplexy. Stereotactic radiotherapy is an alternative for residual tumor or recurrence.

Post-Surgery Complication: Polyuria (problem: Diabetes Insipidus due to damage to posterior pituitary or hypothalamus, leading to ADH deficiency).

sections.title: Diagnosis & Tests: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
content: Clinical Tests: Fatigability (sustained upgaze, repeated blinking), Ice pack test (improves ptosis temporarily), Sleep test (improves ptosis after rest).
Pharmacological Tests: Tensilon (Edrophonium) test (rapid but transient improvement in muscle weakness after IV edrophonium). Must be done with atropine available for cholinergic crisis.
Electrophysiological Tests: Repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response), Single-fiber EMG (increased jitter and blocking).
Antibody Tests: Acetylcholine Receptor (AChR) antibodies (most common), Muscle-Specific Kinase (MuSK) antibodies (for seronegative MG), LRP4 antibodies.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Amblyopia
content: 1. Correct Refractive Error: Prescribe appropriate glasses for significant refractive error or anisometropia (full cycloplegic refraction).
2. Amblyopia Therapy: Initiate immediately after refractive correction if amblyopia persists. Modalities include:
a. Patching: Occlusion of the good eye for several hours daily (e.g., 4-5 hours for moderate amblyopia).
b. Atropine Penalization: Atropine drops in the good eye to blur vision, forcing use of the amblyopic eye.
c. Filters (e.g., Bangerter filters): Applied to glasses over the good eye.
d. Binocular therapy (new approaches): Dichoptic games and virtual reality systems.
3. Follow-up: Regular monitoring to assess visual acuity, compliance, and adjust therapy. Treatment can continue up to 10-12 years of age or even older in some cases.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Convergent Strabismus in a 3-year-old

branches: Accommodative Esotropia (most common cause in this age group, typically with hyperopia)
Acute Esotropia (sudden onset, often with underlying systemic or neurological cause)
Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy (incomitant esotropia, abduction deficit)
Brainstem Tumor (e.g., pontine glioma) - Red Flag!
Hydrocephalus (rare, but can cause 6th nerve palsy)
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD - often associated with infantile ET)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Lateral Rectus Paralysis (6th Nerve Palsy)
content: 1. History & Examination: Onset, progression, duration, systemic diseases (diabetes, HTN, vasculitis), measure angle (prism cover test), check other cranial nerves, AS/PS/pupillary exam.

2. Investigations: Blood sugar, lipid profile. Neuroimaging (MRI brain with contrast) to rule out compressive lesions (tumors, aneurysm) or inflammation/demyelination, especially in younger patients or atypical presentations. If suspected GCA, ESR/CRP.

3. Management (Acute): Observation for 3-6 months (many vasculopathic palsies resolve spontaneously). Patching one eye (to relieve diplopia), prism glasses (Fresnel prisms for temporary, ground-in for stable). Botulinum toxin injection (into ipsilateral medial rectus) to prevent contracture of antagonist and reduce deviation.

4. Management (Chronic/Stable after 6 months): Strabismus surgery (lateral rectus recession + medial rectus resection; vertical muscle transposition if severe) if deviation is stable and non-resolving.

sections.title: Pre-operative Assessment for Cataract Surgery under Local Anesthesia
content: Systemic Diseases: Diabetes, hypertension, cardiac disease, respiratory disease (COPD, asthma), rheumatoid arthritis, bleeding disorders, neurological disorders (Parkinson's, seizures).
Ocular History: Onset, progression, duration of cataract, previous ocular surgery/trauma, any pain/other complaints.
Ocular Examination: Visual acuity, intraocular pressure, anterior segment (cornea, iris, lens), posterior segment (fundus, optic nerve). Check the other eye.
Pupils: Size, shape, reactivity, presence of RAPD.
Extraocular Motility: Assess for strabismus or diplopia.

Fitness for Local Anesthesia: Evaluate patient's ability to lie flat, cooperate, remain still (e.g., not suitable for severe tremors, claustrophobia, active cough). Consider general anesthesia for these cases.

sections.title: Red Flag: Leukocoria in a Child
content: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is a pediatric ophthalmologic emergency.
Most critical differential diagnosis: Retinoblastoma (life-threatening).
Investigations: Examination Under Anesthesia (EUA), B-scan ultrasonography (to assess posterior segment, rule out mass), CT/MRI orbit (for retinoblastoma staging).

Differential Diagnosis for Leukocoria: Retinoblastoma, Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous (PHPV), Congenital Cataract, Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), Coats' Disease, Toxocariasis, Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy (FEVR), Retinal Detachment (especially exudative/tractional).

sections.title: Management of PHPV (Persistent Hyperplastic Primary Vitreous)
content: Anterior PHPV: May present with leukocoria, microphthalmia, shallow AC, cataract, ciliary body processes. Management: Lensectomy/cataract surgery (visual prognosis guarded), amblyopia therapy, watchful for glaucoma.
Posterior PHPV: Retinal fold, tractional RD, optic disc hypoplasia. Management: Vitrectomy to remove fibrotic tissue and prevent RD. Prognosis often poor.
Counseling: Parents need to understand guarded visual prognosis, risk of amblyopia, glaucoma, and retinal detachment, and need for long-term follow-up and amblyopia therapy.

sections.title: Informed Consent: Cataract Surgery Risks
content: Intraoperative: Posterior capsule rupture (PCR), vitreous loss, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, dropped nucleus, iris damage, zonular dialysis.

Postoperative: Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, cystoid macular edema (CME), bullous keratopathy, glaucoma (e.g., pigment dispersion, steroid-induced), persistent uveitis, refractive error, IOL dislocation, secondary membrane formation.

sections.title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) of the Eyelid: Rodent Ulcer
sections.content:
Description: A classic 'rodent ulcer' presents as a raised, pearly nodule with rolled borders, telangiectatic vessels, and often a central ulceration. It is slow-growing but locally invasive.

Most Probable Diagnosis: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common eyelid malignancy.

Treatment: Surgical excision with clear margins (Mohs micrographic surgery is ideal for margin control, especially near critical structures). Reconstruction of the eyelid defect depends on size and location (e.g., direct closure, skin graft, Tenzel flap, Hughes flap, Mustarde flap).

sections.title: Dry Eye Disease: Diagnosis and Management
sections.content:
Stains: Rose Bengal (stains devitalized cells, mucus), Lissamine Green (similar to Rose Bengal, less irritating), Fluorescein (stains corneal epithelial defects).

Other Tests: Tear break-up time (TBUT - measure time from blink to first dry spot), Schirmer test 1 & 2 (tear production), Tear Meniscus Height (TMH - inferior meniscus height at slit lamp), Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) questionnaire.

Treatment Steps:
1. Address Underlying Cause: Systemic diseases (e.g., Sjogren's, thyroid eye disease, rheumatoid arthritis), medications.
2. Environmental Changes: Avoid dry/windy conditions, use humidifiers, frequent blinking, eyelid hygiene (warm compresses, lid scrubs).
3. Artificial Tears: Start with preservative-containing, then shift to preservative-free if needed. Gels/ointments at night.
4. Anti-inflammatory: Topical steroids (short course), Cyclosporine A or Lifitegrast (long-term immunomodulation).
5. Punctal Plugs: To retain natural tears.
6. Systemic Treatment: Doxycycline (for meibomian gland dysfunction - MGD, anti-inflammatory effect), Omega-3 fatty acids.
7. Surgical Options: Tarsorrhaphy (for severe lagophthalmos), correction of entropion/ectropion/trichiasis if contributing.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Facial Nerve Palsy with Lagophthalmos
content: 1. Diagnosis: Confirm facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy, trauma, tumor, infection, stroke). Refer to neurologist for workup.
2. Eye Protection (Temporary Measures): Lubricant eye drops (frequent), lubricant ointments (especially at night), eyelid taping/patching at night, moisture chambers (goggles).
3. Surgical Options (Permanent Measures for prolonged palsy):
a. Medial Canthoplasty: Narrows the palpebral fissure.
b. Lateral Tarsorrhaphy: Temporarily or permanently sutures lateral eyelids together to narrow fissure.
c. Gold Weight Implant: Placed in upper eyelid to aid gravity-assisted lid closure.
d. Lower eyelid tightening procedures (e.g., lateral tarsal strip) for ectropion.
e. Transposition of temporalis muscle for active lid closure.

4. Botulinum Toxin: Can be used in the contralateral orbicularis oculi for symmetry in severe cases or to manage associated tearing due to punctal eversion and reflex tearing (not to treat the palsy itself).
5. Referral: Oculoplastic surgeon for surgical management, neurologist for etiology and systemic management.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis & Management: Child with Lid Swelling and Redness

rows: Eyelid swelling/redness, tenderness. NO proptosis, NO ophthalmoplegia, NO pain on eye movements, NO vision change.
Oral antibiotics (outpatient if mild, no systemic signs). Close monitoring.
Severe eyelid swelling/redness, pain, FEVER, PROPTOSIS, OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, pain on eye movements, decreased vision, RAPD.

URGENT admission, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, CT orbit & sinuses (to check for abscess, differentiate from preseptal), ENT consultation for sinus drainage if needed. Look for optic nerve affection and pupils.
Redness, discharge, lid swelling (mild), usually bilateral. Itching (allergic).
Sudden, bilateral, often itchy, resolves quickly with antihistamines. No pain/fever.
Localized tender lump. Stye (acute infection), Chalazion (chronic inflammation).
Warm compresses, lid hygiene. Incision & drainage if refractory.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Post-Trabeculectomy Hypotony (Shallow AC, Low IOP)
content: 1. Assess: AC depth (grade 1,2,3 - iridocorneal, pupillo-corneal, lenticulo-corneal), Seidel test (bleb leak?), bleb height, fundus (choroidal detachment?). IOP.
2. Differential Diagnosis: Overfiltration (diffuse, flat bleb), Bleb leak (positive Seidel), Ciliary body shutdown (decreased aqueous production), Choroidal detachment (serous or hemorrhagic).
3. Management:
a. Bleb Leak: Aqueous suppressants (if no choroidals), bandage contact lens, patching, ocular lubricants, bleb compression sutures, blood patch, surgical repair.

b. Overfiltration/Ciliary Shutdown (without leak): Cycloplegics (to deepen AC, reduce aqueous flow across ciliary body), viscoelastic injection (to deepen AC), decrease topical steroids, increase antibiotics (prophylactically). Choroidal drainage (only for 'kissing' choroidals threatening macula/optic nerve or chronic effusion, usually avoided for acute serous choroidals).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Malignant Glaucoma (Aqueous Misdirection)
content: 1. Diagnosis: Elevated IOP, shallow/flat AC (often peripheral iridocorneal touch), normal bleb, no pupillary block, no suprachoroidal hemorrhage (confirmed by B-scan).

2. Medical Management: Cycloplegic eye drops (e.g., Atropine 1%), aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), hyperosmotic agents (oral glycerol/isosorbide, IV mannitol). Intensive medical therapy is first-line.

3. Laser Management: If pseudophakic: YAG laser posterior capsulotomy and hyaloidotomy (disrupt anterior vitreous face). If phakic: YAG laser through peripheral iridotomy (to disrupt anterior hyaloid face).

4. Surgical Management: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with anterior hyaloidectomy (often with lensectomy in phakic eyes) to disrupt vitreous integrity and redirect aqueous flow. This is the definitive treatment.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Primary Open Angle Glaucoma (POAG) - Medication Intolerance
content: 1. Initial Treatment: First-line is prostaglandin analog (Latanoprost, Travoprost, Bimatoprost once daily) or beta-blocker (Timolol 0.5% twice daily) if no contraindications.

2. Patient Counseling (Prostaglandin Analogs): Inform about complications (red eye, trichomegaly, iris hyperpigmentation, periocular fat atrophy). Emphasize compliance for a progressive, chronic disease.
3. If Intolerant to Medications:
a. Switch to another class of eye drops (e.g., different prostaglandin, alpha-agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor).
b. Consider Preservative-Free (PF) formulations: Often better tolerated for patients with ocular surface disease or irritation.
c. Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT/ALT): Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT) is a safe and effective option, can be repeated. Reduces IOP by enhancing aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork.
d. Surgical Intervention: If all else fails, consider trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage device (GDD). Especially important for monocular patients or those with advanced disease.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) with Cilioretinal Artery Sparing
content: CRAO is an ocular emergency. Vision loss is sudden and profound. Cilioretinal artery sparing indicates a better prognosis for central vision.
1. Emergency Treatment (within 90-120 minutes of onset):
a. Ocular Massage: Firm digital pressure (10-15s) then rapid release (5-10s) for 5-10 minutes, to dislodge embolus.
b. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Rapidly lowers IOP, potentially dislodging embolus.
c. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy: Limited availability, but can improve oxygenation.
d. Carbogen (95% O2, 5% CO2) or breathing into a paper bag: To induce vasodilation (controversial effectiveness).
e. IOP-lowering drugs: Topical (Timolol), IV (Acetazolamide, Mannitol).
2. Systemic Workup & Referral: URGENT referral to internist/neurologist/cardiologist.
a. Carotid Doppler Ultrasound: To detect carotid artery stenosis (common embolic source).
b. Echocardiogram: To look for cardiac emboli (e.g., atrial fibrillation, valvular disease).
c. Blood tests: ESR/CRP (rule out GCA), coagulation profile, fasting glucose, lipid profile.
d. Check other eye for any signs of vascular disease.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Vitreomacular Traction (VMT)
content: Diagnosis: Confirmed by OCT showing vitreous adherence to the macula.
Treatment Options:
1. Observation: If good vision and no metamorphopsia. Many cases resolve spontaneously.
2. Pharmacological Vitreolysis: Ocriplasmin injection (for focal VMT <1500µm, no epiretinal membrane, phakic eyes).

3. Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): If vision is worsening, severe metamorphopsia, or VMT-related macular complications (e.g., macular hole, cystoid macular edema). May include membrane removal and ILM peeling.

sections.title: Ocular Side Effects of Systemic Medications (Rheumatoid Arthritis)

rows: Posterior Subcapsular Cataract, Glaucoma (steroid-responder), increased infection risk

Baseline exam, annual screening after 5 years or cumulative dose >1000g, or if high risk (renal disease, tamoxifen use). Includes fundus exam, OCT, automated visual fields (10-2), fundus autofluorescence.
Baseline eye exam, monitor for dry eye
Baseline eye exam, monitor for symptoms

sections.title: Glaucomatous Optic Disc Evaluation & CCT
content: Features of Glaucomatous Optic Disc: Large vertical cupping, peripapillary atrophy (alpha and beta zones), nasalization of vessels, bayonetting of vessels, disc hemorrhage, localized or diffuse retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) defects, asymmetry between eyes.

Central Corneal Thickness (CCT) Importance: Thin CCT (<555µm) can lead to underestimation of IOP by Goldmann applanation tonometry, increasing glaucoma risk. Thick CCT (>588µm) can lead to overestimation. Normal CCT is ~550µm.

Investigations: Full glaucoma evaluation includes IOP measurement, gonioscopy, optic disc evaluation (clinical + stereo photos), visual field testing (HVF), OCT of RNFL and optic disc, pachymetry (CCT).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Myasthenia Gravis (MG)
content: 1. Pharmacological: Pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) for symptomatic relief. Oral steroids (e.g., prednisone) for immunosuppression. Other immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil).
2. Thymectomy: Often considered for generalized MG, especially with thymoma.
3. Crisis Management: Plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) for myasthenic crisis.
4. Referral: Neurologist for diagnosis, workup (AChR antibodies, EMG, Tensilon test, CT chest for thymoma), and long-term systemic management.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Causes of DCR Tube Indications

branches: Secondary Acquired Lacrimal Obstruction (SALDO - e.g., trauma, inflammation, tumors)
Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (persistent after probing/balloon dilation)

sections.title: Complications of DCR (Dacryocystorhinostomy)
content: Bleeding (intra- or post-operative)
Infection
Failure of lacrimal drainage (most common, due to fibrosis/scarring)
Nasal synechiae
CSF leak (rare with external DCR)
Diplopia (rare)
Dislodgement of tube (if intubation performed)

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Phthisis Bulbi Causes
Management of Phthisis Bulbi (Cosmetic Options)
content: Colored Contact Lenses (if globe integrity allows and some vision remains)
Prosthetic Shell (scleral shell) for cosmesis over a phthisical eye.

Evisceration with Orbital Implant: Removes contents of the globe, leaving scleral shell, then implant placed to restore orbital volume, followed by a prosthetic eye shell. Preferred over enucleation for phthisis due to better motility and volume.

sections.title: Complications of Scleral Fixation IOL (SFIOL)
content: Intraocular Hemorrhage (hyphema, vitreous hemorrhage)
IOP elevation/Glaucoma (due to trauma, inflammation, cyclodialysis, PAS)
Infection (endophthalmitis)
IOL Decentration/Tilt/Dislocation
Suture-related complications (suture erosion, breakage, knot exposure, inflammation)
Retinal Detachment
Cystoid Macular Edema
Corneal Edema
Diplopia

sections.title: Management Protocol: IOL Subluxation
content: 1. Assessment: Visual acuity, IOP, type of IOL, degree of subluxation, presence of vitreous in AC.
2. Conservative Management: If vision is good and minimal symptoms: observation, glasses, contact lenses.
3. Surgical Management: If vision is poor, diplopia, or IOL rubbing iris/cornea (causing inflammation/glaucoma):
a. Repositioning (if possible, e.g., with iris hooks or viscodissection).
b. Exchange for a new IOL (ACIOL, iris-fixated, scleral-fixated).
c. Removal of IOL and leave aphakic (then secondary IOL later).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK)

branches: Endothelial Cell Loss (from complicated cataract surgery)
Trauma (e.g., intra-capsular cataract extraction (ICCE) or complicated extra-capsular cataract extraction (ECCCE) with extensive iris loss)
IOL rubbing on endothelium (e.g., ACIOL, misplaced PCIOL)
Pre-existing endothelial dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy)

sections.title: Corneal Graft Options for PBK
content: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): Full-thickness corneal replacement. Indicated if stromal scarring is significant.
Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK/DSAEK): Partial-thickness replacement of endothelium. Preferred if stroma is clear.
Combined Procedure: Graft + IOL implantation (if aphakic or IOL malpositioned).
Staged Procedure: Graft first, then IOL implantation later.
Aphakic Contact Lens: For correction if no IOL is placed and surgery is deferred.

sections.title: Complications of Endothelial Keratoplasty (EK)
content: Graft Detachment (most common, requires rebubbling)
Primary Graft Failure
Graft Rejection
IOP elevation/Glaucoma
Infection
Pupillary block
Retinal detachment (rare)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Full Thickness Macular Hole
content: Grading (Gass classification): Stage 1 (foveal cyst/split), Stage 2 (partial break), Stage 3 (full thickness with operculum), Stage 4 (full thickness with PVD).
Causes: Vitreomacular traction (most common), trauma, high myopia, inflammation.
Surgery: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) with Internal Limiting Membrane (ILM) peeling and gas tamponade.
Gas Injection: Types (SF6, C2F6, C3F8), complications (pupillary block glaucoma, cataract), precautions (face-down positioning, no air travel).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with Macular Edema
content: Diagnosis: Fundus exam (NVD, NVE, vitreous hemorrhage), FA, OCT (for macular edema, VMT).
1. Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) Laser: First-line for PDR (neovascularization), settings typically 500µm spot size, 0.1s duration, 200-500mW power, 1200-1600 spots over multiple sessions.
2. Vitrectomy Indications for Diabetes: Persistent vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula, combined rhegmatogenous and tractional RD.
3. Silicone Oil in Vitrectomy: Complications (glaucoma, band keratopathy, cataract), duration (ideally 3-6 months, but longer for complex cases).
4. Macular Edema (CME) Management:
a. Intravitreal Injections: Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) are first-line, or steroid implants (Dexamethasone, Fluocinolone).

b. Vitreomacular Traction (VMT) with Macular Edema: Intravitreal injections are CONTRAINDICATED or less effective. Laser may increase traction. Vitrectomy to remove membrane and relieve traction is preferred.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Congenital Optic Disc Anomalies

branches: Glaucomatous Optic Disc (can be congenital or developmental glaucoma)

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Alternating Exotropia & Inferior Oblique Overaction
content: Alternating Exotropia: Deviation of one eye outwards, then the other. Indicates good vision in both eyes and alternation of fixation.
Inferior Oblique Overaction (IOOA): Eye elevates and abducts excessively on attempted adduction. Often associated with V-pattern strabismus.
Management: Refractive correction, amblyopia treatment if unilateral, then surgical correction (bilateral lateral rectus recession, +/- inferior oblique weakening procedures for IOOA).

sections.title: Investigation Workup: Optic Neuropathy (RAPD, Cupped Disc, Pallor)
content: Visual Acuity, Color Vision (dyschromatopsia), Visual Fields (e.g., automated perimetry for specific defects).
Pupil Exam: RAPD (afferent pupillary defect) indicates asymmetric optic nerve damage.
Fundus Exam: Optic disc for pallor, cupping, swelling, atrophy. Assess RNFL.
OCT of Optic Nerve Head (ONH) and RNFL: Quantifies nerve fiber layer thickness and disc changes, useful for monitoring progression.

Systemic Workup: Depending on suspected cause – ESR/CRP (GCA), MRI Brain/Orbit (compressive, inflammatory, demyelinating lesions), autoantibodies (NMO, sarcoidosis), infectious workup (syphilis, Lyme).
Types of Optic Atrophy: Primary (e.g., hereditary, compressive), Secondary (e.g., post-papilledema), Consecutive (e.g., post-retinal disease), Glaucomatous (distinct cupping pattern).

sections.title: Management Protocol: Dislocated IOL with Pupillary Block and Iris Bombe
content: 1. Diagnosis: Slit lamp exam (IOL optic in AC, iris bombe, peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), pigments on IOL), IOP measurement.
2. Effects: High IOP (due to pupillary block, PAS), corneal endothelial damage (from IOL contact), inflammation.
3. Emergency Management: Topical aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, CAIs), cycloplegics (to dilate pupil and break block), hyperosmotic agents (oral glycerol/IV mannitol).
4. Definitive Management:
a. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): To relieve pupillary block if the block is between iris and lens.
b. Surgical Repositioning/Exchange: If LPI fails or IOL causing endothelial damage. Repositioning or exchange to ACIOL, iris-fixated IOL, or scleral-fixated IOL.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Corneal Decompensation Post-Cataract Surgery

branches: Pre-existing endothelial dystrophy (e.g., Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy)
Endothelial cell loss during complicated surgery
IOL trauma to endothelium (e.g., ACIOL, IOL subluxation)
Cystoid macular edema (indirectly affecting vision, but not corneal decompensation)

sections.title: Management Protocol: Macular Edema (General)
content: 1. Confirm Diagnosis: OCT (gold standard), fundus exam, FA.
2. Treat Underlying Cause: Diabetes (control blood sugar, BP, lipids), RVO (laser, anti-VEGF), inflammation (steroids).
3. Intravitreal Injections: Anti-VEGF agents (Bevacizumab, Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) for DME, RVO, nAMD. Steroid implants (Dexamethasone, Fluocinolone) for refractory or non-VEGF driven edema.
4. Laser: Focal/grid laser for non-center-involving DME or some RVOs (less common now).
5. Vitrectomy: For macular edema with significant vitreomacular traction (VMT) or epiretinal membrane (ERM).

sections.title: Red Flag: Unilateral Large Peripheral Visual Field Defect
content: Cause: Needs urgent neuro-ophthalmic evaluation.
Differential Diagnosis:
1. Optic Neuropathy (e.g., AION, compressive lesion): Severe damage to optic nerve head, can cause altitudinal or diffuse defects.
2. Retinal Detachment: Peripheral RD can cause a dense, sharp-bordered field defect corresponding to the detached area.
3. Retinoschisis: Can cause absolute or relative field defects, typically stable.
4. Chorioretinal Scars/Lesions: Large lesions (e.g., choroidal melanoma, toxoplasmosis scar) can cause corresponding field loss.
5. Stroke/Tumor in Optic Radiations or Occipital Cortex: Typically respecting vertical or horizontal meridians (e.g., homonymous hemianopia).

sections.title: Cosmetic Options for Phthisis Bulbi with Enophthalmic Deep Sulcus
content: Prosthetic Shell (scleral shell): Worn over the existing phthisical globe.
Evisceration with Orbital Implant: Removes globe contents, replaces with implant to restore volume, then custom prosthetic eye.
Enucleation with Orbital Implant: Removes entire globe. Often necessary if phthisis is painful or risk of sympathetic ophthalmia.
Volume Augmentation: Injectable fillers (fat, hyaluronic acid) or implants (dermofat graft) into the anophthalmic socket or deep superior sulcus to improve appearance.

sections.title: Keratoconus: Vogt Striae and Management
content: Vogt Striae: Fine, vertical, whitish lines in the deep stroma/Descemet's membrane, parallel to the cone axis. Disappear with digital pressure.
Other signs: Munson's sign, Rizzuti's sign, Fleischer's ring, irregular astigmatism, corneal thinning, apical scarring.
Management of Keratoconus:
1. Optical Correction: Glasses, then rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses (gold standard for visual rehabilitation). Scleral lenses for advanced cases or intolerance to RGP.
2. Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL): To halt progression in early to moderate disease.
3. Intracorneal Ring Segments (ICRS/Intacs): To reduce corneal steepness and improve vision.
4. Keratoplasty: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) or Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) for advanced cases with significant scarring or poor vision with contact lenses.

Management of Acute Hydrops: Cycloplegics, topical steroids, topical hyperosmotic agents (e.g., Muro 128), aqueous suppressants (if IOP elevated). May inject gas (SF6) into AC to tamponade Descemet's tear. Requires close follow-up.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with Ahmed Valve
content: 1. Diagnosis: History of ischemic vascular disease (e.g., PDR, CRVO), rubeosis iridis, elevated IOP, gonioscopy shows neovascularization of angle.

2. Initial Management: Treat underlying cause (PRP, anti-VEGF injections - for rapid NVI regression and to reduce surgical inflammation), topical anti-glaucoma medications (avoid miotics), topical steroids.
3. Ahmed Valve Implantation: Often necessary for refractory NVG. It's a glaucoma drainage device that shunts aqueous from AC to a subconjunctival reservoir.
4. Post-Ahmed Valve: Continue anti-VEGF if rubeosis persists, topical steroids, aqueous suppressants until IOP stabilizes.

5. Next Eye NVG: If one eye has NVG, the other eye is at high risk. Close monitoring of the fellow eye (fundus exam, IOP, gonioscopy) is crucial. Prophylactic PRP may be considered if signs of severe ischemia.

sections.title: Management Protocol: Corneal Trauma with Anterior Synechiae
content: 1. Initial Assessment: Rule out ruptured globe (Seidel test), assess vision, IOP, AC depth, extent of synechiae.

2. Medical Management: Cycloplegics (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) to prevent further synechiae formation and reduce inflammation. Topical steroids (to reduce inflammation). Topical antibiotics (prophylactically if epithelial defect). IOP lowering agents if elevated.
3. Surgical Management: If synechiae are extensive, causing pupillary distortion, glaucoma, or corneal endothelial damage:
a. Synechiolysis: Surgical separation of adhesions (e.g., using a cyclodialysis spatula, fine instrument).
b. Reconstructive surgery: If iris damage is severe.
c. Glaucoma surgery: If secondary glaucoma persists despite synechiolysis and medical therapy.

sections.title: Investigation Workup: Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO)
content: Fundus Exam: Retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, dilated tortuous veins in a sector.
OCT: Macular edema, intraretinal fluid, subretinal fluid, epiretinal membrane, retinal thickening.
Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Shows non-perfusion (ischemia), macular edema, leakage from vessels, neovascularization.
Systemic Workup: Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, glaucoma, hypercoagulable states (less common for BRVO than CRVO). Refer to internist.

sections.title: Follow-up for PDR with PRP Scars and Neovascularization (Stable)
content: Frequency: Typically every 3-6 months if stable (no active neovascularization, no significant vitreous hemorrhage, well-controlled macular edema).
Closer Follow-up: Every 1-3 months if any signs of progression (new NV, recurrent VH, worsening ME), or if systemic control is poor.
Monitoring: Fundus exam (check for new NV, re-evaluate PRP completeness), OCT (for ME, VMT), IOP (secondary glaucoma).
